claim: Anatomical and physiological studies have led to the assumption that the dorsal striatum receives exclusively excitatory afferents from the cortex.
source: Anatomical and physiological studies have led to the assumption that the dorsal striatum receives exclusively excitatory afferents from the cortex.
evidence: This claim references established scientific consensus based on prior anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: The cortex, via corticostriatal somatostatin neurons (CS-SOM), has a direct inhibitory influence on the output of the striatum SPNs.
source: We found that the cortex, via corticostriatal somatostatin neurons (CS-SOM), has a direct inhibitory influence on the output of the striatum SPNs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cortical neurons regulate the activity of spiny projection neurons (SPNs) in the striatum through long-range glutamatergic/excitatory projections.
source: It is very well established that cortical neurons regulate the activity of spiny projection neurons (SPNs) in the striatum through long-range glutamatergic/excitatory projections (Landry et al., 1984; Wilson, 1987; 2004; Graybiel et al., 1994; Lovinger and Tyler, 1996; Reiner et al., 2003; Kress et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Inhibition in the striatum is mediated by local feed-forward and feed-back circuits.
source: while inhibition is mediated by local feed-forward and feed-back circuits (for review [Tepper et al., 2008]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The feed-forward circuit is characterized by GABAergic striatal interneurons that receive excitatory inputs from the cortex and monosynaptically inhibit SPNs.
source: The feed-forward circuit is characterized by GABAergic striatal interneurons that receive excitatory inputs from the cortex and monosynaptically inhibit SPNs.
evidence: This claim describes established knowledge about striatal circuit organization.

claim: The feed-back circuit is characterized by SPNs and their interconnections via local axon collaterals.
source: The feed-back circuit is characterized by SPNs and their interconnections via local axon collaterals (Calabresi et al., 1991; Kawaguchi, 1993; Kita, 1993; 1996; Kawaguchi et al., 1995; Mallet et al., 2005; Planert et al., 2010; Ibanez-Sandoval et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Striatal neuronal activity has been shown to be involved in movement, learning, and goal-directed behavior.
source: Because striatal neuronal activity has been shown to be involved in movement, learning, and goal-directed behavior (Graybiel, 1995; Schultz et al., 2003; Barnes et al., 2005; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Between 1–10% of the GABAergic 'interneurons' in rodents, cats, and monkeys also give rise to long-range corticocortical projections.
source: Anatomical studies using retrograde tracers and immunohistochemistry have proposed that between 1–10% of the GABAergic 'interneurons' in rodents, cats, and monkeys also give rise to long-range corticocortical projections (McDonald and Burkhalter, 1993; Tomioka et al., 2005; Higo et al., 2007; Tomioka and Rockland, 2007; Higo et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Many long-range corticocortical projections arise from somatostatin-expressing neurons.
source: A growing body of evidence suggests that many of these projections arise from somatostatin-expressing neurons (Tomioka et al., 2005; Higo et al., 2007; Tomioka and Rockland, 2007; Higo et al., 2009; McDonald et al., 2012; Melzer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: A previous study has demonstrated the presence of a corticostriatal GABAergic projection.
source: A previous study has demonstrated the presence of a corticostriatal GABAergic projection (Tomioka et al., 2015), but the cells of origin and physiological function of this GABAergic projection from the cortex to the dorsal striatum were not explored.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The cells of origin and physiological function of the GABAergic projection from the cortex to the dorsal striatum were not explored in previous studies.
source: A previous study has demonstrated the presence of a corticostriatal GABAergic projection (Tomioka et al., 2015), but the cells of origin and physiological function of this GABAergic projection from the cortex to the dorsal striatum were not explored.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in prior research that the current study addresses.

claim: GFP was colocalized with SOM/tdTomato-expressing neurons in the auditory cortex.
source: GFP was colocalized with SOM/tdTomato-expressing neurons in the AC (Figure 1b left)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: GFP-positive axons were visible in coronal sections of the right dorsal striatum.
source: GFP-positive axons were visible in coronal sections of the right dorsal striatum in these mice (Figure 1b middle and right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: CS-SOM neurons were present primarily in layers 5 and 6 of the auditory cortex.
source: CS-SOM neurons were retrogradely labelled with GFP, and their somata were present primarily in layers 5 and 6 of the AC (Figure 1d, middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: CS-SOM neurons are similar to SOM interneurons in their morphology and send an axonal projection into the subcortical white matter.
source: Confocal images of biocytin-filled CS-SOM neurons showed that they are similar to SOM interneurons in their morphology and send an axonal projection into the subcortical white matter (Figure 1d, right; Neurolucida-reconstructed CS-SOM neuron Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1d and 1e.

claim: CS-SOM neurons have a wide action potential and low rheobase.
source: These properties include a wide action potential and low rheobase (the smallest current step evoking an action potential) (Figure 1f, top; action potentials in CS-SOM neurons, shown in black, are wider than those from fast-spiking interneurons, example in red).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The responses to current steps in CS-SOM neurons were typical for SOM interneurons.
source: The responses to current steps in CS-SOM neurons were typical for SOM interneurons (Figure 1f, bottom; notice the sag from a hyperpolarizing current step).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

source: Basic electrophysiological properties for CS-SOM neurons (n = 13) included (Figure 1g): resting membrane potential, −72.93 ± 1.16 mV
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: CS-SOM neurons have an input resistance of 240 ± 26.98 MΩ.
source: input resistance, 240 ± 26.98 MΩ

claim: CS-SOM neurons have a membrane time constant of 6.84 ± 0.71 ms.
source: membrane time constant, 6.84 ± 0.71 ms

claim: CS-SOM neurons have a rheobase of 100 ± 15pA.
source: rheobase, 100 ± 15pA

claim: CS-SOM neurons have an action potential threshold of −41.35 ± 1.33 mV.
source: action potential threshold, −41.35 ± 1.33 mV
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: CS-SOM neurons have an action potential height of 54.18 ± 2.21 mV.
source: action potential height, 54.18 ± 2.21 mV
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: CS-SOM neurons have an action potential width of 0.49 ± 0.05 ms.
source: action potential width, 0.49 ± 0.05 ms

claim: CS-SOM neurons have an F-I slope of 0.24 ± 0.03 Hz/pA step.
source: F-I slope, 0.24 ± 0.03 Hz/pA step.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: AAV1.Flex viral vectors exhibited both anterograde and retrograde transfection capabilities.
source: Although, in our experience, AAV1.Flex viral vectors (Atasoy et al., 2008) exhibited both anterograde and retrograde (Rothermel et al., 2013) transfection capabilities
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: When AAV1.Flex virus was injected in the cortex, only anterograde labeling of CS-SOM neurons was observed.
source: when we injected this virus in the cortex we only observed anterograde labeling of CS-SOM neurons (i.e. no SOM somata transfected in the dorsal striatum; see Figure 1b, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: When AAV1.Flex virus was injected into the dorsal striatum, transfected SOM somata were observed both in the dorsal striatum and in the cortex.
source: In contrast, when we injected this virus into the dorsal striatum, we observed transfected SOM somata both in the dorsal striatum (Figure 1d, left) and in the cortex (Figure 1d, middle left and middle right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The inhibitory projection from cortex to striatum is unidirectional, arising preferentially from layer 5 and 6 SOM neurons in the cortex which project to the dorsal striatum.
source: These data show that this inhibitory projection is unidirectional, arising preferentially from layer 5 and 6 SOM neurons in the cortex which project to the dorsal striatum.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on viral transfection patterns.

claim: ChR2-positive axons remain photoexcitable even when severed from their parent somata.
source: These axons have been reported to remain photoexcitable even when severed from their parent somata (Petreanu et al., 2007; Rock and Apicella, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The IPSCs onset of the photo-evoked response was 2.2 ± 0.11 ms.
source: The IPSCs onset of the photo-evoked response was 2.2 ± 0.11 ms (Figure 2g, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The latency of 2.2 ± 0.11 ms is consistent with the IPSCs being the result of a monosynaptic inhibitory input from the cortex.
source: This latency is consistent with the IPSCs being the result of a monosynaptic inhibitory input from the cortex and not a local striatal feedback inhibitory network recruited by cortical projections.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the measured latency data.

claim: Blocking excitatory neurotransmission by application of glutamate receptor antagonists NBQX and CPP did not abolish the CS-SOM-ChR2-evoked synaptic IPSCs.
source: Blocking excitatory neurotransmission by application of glutamate receptor antagonists NBQX and CPP did not abolish the CS-SOM-ChR2-evoked synaptic IPSCs (Figure 2f, magenta trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Blocking inhibitory neurotransmission by application of gabazine completely abolished the CS-SOM-ChR2-evoked synaptic IPSCs.
source: In contrast, blocking inhibitory neurotransmission by application of gabazine (Figure 2f, black trace) completely abolished the CS-SOM-ChR2-evoked synaptic IPSCs, confirming they were elicited by direct cortical inhibitory transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: CS-SOM-ChR2-evoked synaptic IPSCs have a peak of 122 ± 26 pA.
source: Basic biophysical properties for CS-SOM-ChR2-evoked synaptic IPSCs (n = 16) included (Figure 2g,h,i): peak, 122 ± 26 pA
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: CS-SOM-ChR2-evoked synaptic IPSCs have a charge of 3.85 ± 0.67 pC.

claim: CS-SOM-ChR2-evoked synaptic IPSCs have a decay time of 28.87 ± 2.76 ms.

claim: A large proportion of striatal SPNs receive direct inhibitory input driven by CS-SOM neurons.
source: These data reveal that a large proportion of striatal SPNs receive direct inhibitory input driven by CS-SOM neurons but does not exclude the possibility that other striatal neurons also receive inhibitory input from these projections.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Combining current injection with photoactivation of CS-SOM ChR2-positive axons resulted in a delay of the first action potential.
source: Combining current injection with photoactivation of CS-SOM ChR2-positive axons, we observed a delay of the first action potential (Figure 2j, blue traces), with an average delay of 159.16 ± 66.45 ms (n=6) (Figure 2k).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2j and 2k.

claim: The average delay of the first action potential was 159.16 ± 66.45 ms.
source: with an average delay of 159.16 ± 66.45 ms (n=6) (Figure 2k).

claim: CS-SOM projections act directly on SPNs and have the ability to affect spike generation and timing in these neurons.
source: Overall, these results indicate that CS-SOM projections act directly on SPNs and have the ability to affect spike generation and timing in these neurons.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Direct pathway SPNs (dSPNs) express D1-type dopamine receptors.
source: Direct pathway SPNs (dSPNs) express D1-type dopamine receptors and are suggested to promote behaviors that have previously been rewarded.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about striatal pathways.

claim: Direct pathway SPNs are suggested to promote behaviors that have previously been rewarded.
source: Direct pathway SPNs (dSPNs) express D1-type dopamine receptors and are suggested to promote behaviors that have previously been rewarded.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about striatal pathways.

claim: Indirect pathway SPNs (iSPNs) express D2-type dopamine receptors.
source: On the other hand, indirect pathway SPNs (iSPNs) express D2-type dopamine receptors and are suggested to suppress behaviors that have not previously been rewarded (Gong et al., 2003; Ade et al., 2011; Calabresi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Indirect pathway SPNs are suggested to suppress behaviors that have not previously been rewarded.
source: On the other hand, indirect pathway SPNs (iSPNs) express D2-type dopamine receptors and are suggested to suppress behaviors that have not previously been rewarded (Gong et al., 2003; Ade et al., 2011; Calabresi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In Drd1a-tdTomato and Drd2-EGFP mice, fluorescent labeling is restricted to SPNs.
source: It has been reported (Ade et al., 2011) that in Drd1a-tdTomato and Drd2-EGFP mice, fluorescent labeling is restricted to SPNs (i.e. no fluorescent labeling of the three main classes of interneurons in the striatum: parvalbumin-expressing, somatostatin-expressing, and cholinergic).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Six out of fourteen neurons were recovered after patching and were processed for imaging in the D1/D2 experiments.
source: Six out of fourteen neurons were recovered after patching and were processed for imaging; all six of these neurons showed a high density of dendritic spines at 40-63X magnification.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: There were no differences in IPSCs rise times between dSPNs and iSPNs.
source: There were no differences in IPSCs rise times (Figure 3g; example IPSCs from iSPN Figure 3f), suggesting the CS-SOM synapses had similar somatodendritic distributions on dSPNs and iSPNs.

source: Together, these results indicate that CS-SOM neurons do not preferentially innervate dSPNs vs. iSPNs in the dorsal striatum.

source: charge, 3.58 ± 0.59 pC

source: rise time, 1.76 ± 0.14 ms
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4h.

source: decay time, 32.96 ± 4.98 ms.

claim: Three out of nine neurons from motor cortex experiments were recovered after patching and were processed for imaging.
source: Three out of nine neurons were recovered after patching and were processed for imaging; all three of these neurons showed dendritic spines at 40-63X magnification.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental procedure and results.

claim: All three recovered neurons from motor cortex experiments showed dendritic spines at 40-63X magnification.
source: all three of these neurons showed dendritic spines at 40-63X magnification.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from imaging.

claim: In motor cortex, as well as in auditory cortex, CS-SOM projections act directly on SPNs.
source: Overall, these results indicate that in MC, as well as in AC, CS-SOM projections act directly on SPNs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from both cortical areas.

claim: Both the motor and the auditory cortices send long-range GABAergic projections to the dorsal striatum, via CS-SOM neurons.
source: Our results support this hypothesis and additionally conclude that both the motor and the auditory cortices send long-range GABAergic projections to the dorsal striatum, via CS-SOM neurons (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The corticostriatal somatostatin projection connectivity pattern is likely a general feature of the corticostriatal network.
source: Because of its presence in two such disparate cortical areas, this would suggest that the corticostriatal somatostatin projection connectivity pattern is likely a general feature of the corticostriatal network.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation of the projection in multiple cortical areas.

claim: CS-SOM neurons provide a major GABAergic projection to the dorsal striatum.
source: Our results suggest that CS-SOM neurons provide a major GABAergic projection to the dorsal striatum, in agreement with a recent anatomical study in the mouse frontal cortex (Tomioka et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's data and a citation to prior research.

claim: Previous results from retrospinal and somatosensory cortex have provided anatomical evidence for expression of parvalbumin in glutamatergic and GABAergic pathways in mice.
source: However previous results from retrospinal and somatosensory cortex (Jinno and Kosaka, 2004) have provided anatomical evidence for expression of parvalbumin in glutamatergic and GABAergic pathways in mice suggesting that corticostriatal long-range inhibitory neurons are characterized predominantly by parvalbumin-expressing neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Recent results from prefrontal cortex show that corticostriatal long-range inhibitory neurons are characterized predominantly by parvalbumin-expressing or vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing but not somatostatin-expressing interneurons.
source: Moreover, recent results from prefrontal cortex (Lee et al., 2014), show that corticostriatal long-range inhibitory neurons are characterized predominantly by parvalbumin-expressing or vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing but not somatostatin-expressing interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Corticostriatal long-range GABAergic projections may be characterized by heterogeneous subtypes of interneurons.
source: Overall, these suggest that corticostriatal long-range GABAergic projections may be characterized by heterogeneous subtypes of interneurons, and that additional studies are necessary to determine the subtypes and the physiological impact of long-range corticostriatal GABAergic projections on striatal neurons.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the comparison of the current study with prior research.

claim: CS-SOM neurons target SPNs and have the ability to affect their spike timing and generation.
source: Particularly, CS-SOM neurons target SPNs and have the ability to affect their spike timing and generation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: In the cortex, interneurons target the somatodendritic compartment of pyramidal neurons.
source: In the cortex, interneurons target the somatodendritic compartment of pyramidal neurons (Somogyi et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: SOM cortical and striatal interneurons target the dendrites of pyramidal neurons and SPNs, respectively.
source: SOM cortical and striatal interneurons in particular target the dendrites of pyramidal neurons and SPNs, respectively; although not specifically tuft dendrites as is characteristic of their hippocampal analogue, OLM cells (Freund and Buzsaki, 1996; Kubota and Kawaguchi, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CS-SOM neurons, by targeting the dendrites of SPNs, play a role in the integration of incoming cortical excitatory inputs to the striatum.
source: We suggest that a similar inhibitory mechanism might be applied to the corticostriatal long-range inhibitory circuit, in which CS-SOM neurons, by targeting the dendrites of SPNs, play a role in the integration of incoming cortical excitatory inputs to the striatum.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the study's findings and prior knowledge.

claim: Long-range glutamatergic/excitatory projections regulate the activity of dSPNs and iSPNs.
source: It is very well established that long-range glutamatergic/excitatory projections regulate the activity of dSPNs and iSPNs.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge.

claim: The cortex provides an inhibitory projection to both direct and indirect pathway neurons.
source: Our results show that the cortex provides an inhibitory projection to both direct and indirect pathway neurons, influencing the output of both striatal networks involved in action selection and suppression of action.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The functional role of inhibition from CS-SOM neurons might be in shaping the output of both direct and indirect pathways rather than separating their activity.
source: The functional role of inhibition from CS-SOM neurons might be not in separating the activity of direct and indirect striatal pathways, but rather in shaping the output of both.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: Long-range excitatory corticostriatal connections from intratelencephalic and pyramidal tract neurons in motor cortex are made onto both dSPNs and iSPNs in the mouse dorsal striatum.
source: This is reminiscent of the finding by Kress et al. (Kress et al., 2013) that long-range excitatory corticostriatal connections from intratelencephalic and pyramidal tract neurons in motor cortex are made onto both dSPNs and iSPNs in the mouse dorsal striatum.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The dorsal striatum is a brain structure where functionally distinct cortical regions converge.
source: The dorsal striatum is a brain structure where functionally distinct cortical regions (e.g. motor, auditory, visual, somatosensory) converge (Wilson et al., 1983; Schneider, 1991; Flaherty and Graybiel, 1993; Chudler et al., 1995; Reig and Silberberg, 2014; Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Information reaching the dorsal striatum via the corticostriatal projection is either channeled into parallel functional segregated circuits or integrated within these circuits.
source: Anatomical and physiological data have suggested that once this information reaches the dorsal striatum via the corticostriatal projection, it is either channeled into parallel functional segregated circuits (Alexander et al., 1986; Bordi and LeDoux, 1992; Bordi et al., 1993; Parent and Hazrati, 1995; Middleton and Strick, 2000) or integrated within these circuits (Nauta and Domesick, 1984; Hoffer and Alloway, 2001; Kolomiets et al., 2001; Reig and Silberberg, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The existence of direct inhibitory cortical inputs to the dorsal striatum is likely to have profound consequences for corticostriatal mechanisms.
source: The existence of direct inhibitory cortical inputs to the dorsal striatum is likely to have profound consequences for corticostriatal mechanisms by which the AC regulates the output of the striatum and how auditory information is transformed into motor command (Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: The dorsal striatum is characterized by activity-dependent plasticity.
source: It is very well established that the dorsal striatum is characterized by activity-dependent plasticity (for review, see [Kreitzer and Malenka, 2008]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Striatal plasticity can alter the transfer of information throughout the striatum and may serve as a neuronal substrate for the transformation of sensory information and motor planning for flexible motor actions and procedural memory.
source: Particularly, striatal plasticity can alter the transfer of information throughout the striatum and may serve as a neuronal substrate for the transformation of sensory information and motor planning for flexible motor actions and procedural memory.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about striatal plasticity.

claim: Neurons in the dorsal striatum of the rat are selectively potentiated by auditory corticostriatal neurons to promote the learned transformation of sounds into motor actions.
source: Recently, Xiong et al. (Xiong et al., 2015) found that auditory corticostriatal projections are involved in the learning of an auditory frequency discrimination task. They found that neurons in the dorsal striatum of the rat are selectively potentiated by auditory corticostriatal neurons to promote the learned transformation of sounds into motor actions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Motor learning is characterized by structural rearrangements of presynaptic boutons of cortical SOM interneurons.
source: Moreover, Chen et al. (Chen et al., 2015) demonstrated that motor learning is characterized by structural rearrangements of presynaptic boutons of cortical SOM interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CS-SOM neurons might play a role in mechanisms underlying spine dynamics by inducing a specific reorganization of dendritic excitatory synapses on SPNs.
source: Further experiments are needed to understand the functional significance of this direct cortical inhibition to the dorsal striatum, but in combination with the two above mentioned studies it invites speculation that CS-SOM neurons might play a role in mechanisms underlying spine dynamics by inducing a specific reorganization of dendritic excitatory synapses on SPNs and have consequences on learning and/or memory retrieval.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the study's findings and prior research.

claim: The dorsal striatum receives not only glutamatergic excitatory inputs from the cortex, but also inhibitory inputs.
source: We have shown that the dorsal striatum receives not only glutamatergic excitatory inputs from the cortex, but also inhibitory inputs.
evidence: This claim is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The timing and ratio of excitation and inhibition can dynamically affect the output of the dorsal striatum, providing a general mechanism for motor control driven by sensory stimuli.
source: This may suggest that the timing and ratio of excitation and inhibition, two opposing forces in the mammalian cerebral cortex, can dynamically affect the output of the dorsal striatum, providing a general mechanism for motor control driven by sensory stimuli.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the study's findings.
